newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Australian, Swiss win Nobel prize for cell research.
newsitem.headline: Australian, Swiss win Nobel prize for cell research.

text.p: Two scientists, a Swiss and an Australian, shared the 1996 Nobel Medicine Prize for discoveries made while working in Australia on how the body detects virus- infected cells, Sweden's Karolinska Institute said on Monday.
The winners were Peter Doherty, 55, born in Australia and now working at the University of Tennessee in Memphis and Rolf Zinkernagel, 52, Swiss-born and now working at the University of Zurich.

The two men will share $1.12 million as their prize. Doherty began his career as a veterinary officer at Brisbane's Animal Research Institute after attending universities in the Australian state of Queensland and Edinburgh, Scotland.
He is now chairman of the Department of Immunology at St Jude Children's Research Hospital, Memphis, Tennessee, and a professor at the University of Tennessee's College of Medicine.
Zinkernagel is head of the Institute of Experimental Immunology at the University of Zurich.
Zinkernagel, born in Basel, Switzerland, studied in his home town and in Canberra, where he worked with Doherty.

The institute said the scientists' work at the John Curtin School of Medical Research in Canberra from 1973 to 1975 had been crucial for understanding the mechanisms used by humans to recognise foreign bodies.
"The discovery is therefore highly relevant to clinical medicine.

"It relates both to efforts to strengthen the immune response against invading microorganisms and certain forms of cancer, and to efforts to diminish the effects of autoimmune reactions in inflammatory diseases, such as rheumatic conditions, multiple sclerosis and diabetes," it added.
"Where infectious diseases are concerned, the new knowledge provides a better platform for the construction of new vaccines," the institute said in a statement announcing the awards.
In Canberra, Zinkernagel and Doherty used mice to study how the immune system and particularly T-lympocytes -- which protect the body against infection -- protected animals.
Infected mice developed "killer lymphocytes", which in a test tube could kill cells that had been infected with a virus.
The two men made another unexpected discovery -- that the lymphocytes were only active against a specific virus in a specific mouse and would not protect a different animal.
"Zinkernagel's and Doherty's findings had an immediate impact on immunological research," the institute said.
